 In Tyler We Trust: Meet the Rising Stars of Camp Flog Gnaw 2026
 In Tyler We Trust: Meet the Rising Stars of Camp Flog Gnaw 2026
 Rio Amor, Natanya, 54 Ultra, Gabriel Jacoby, Quadeca, and Nomi talk about their upcoming sets, their festival packing lists, and what Camp Flog Gnaw means to their emerging careers.
 WORDS BY RISA KOEHLER
 Tyler, the Creator has never treated Camp Flog Gnaw Carnival as just a lineup — it’s a statement of taste. What began in 2012 as a small one-day event is now on the festival’s 12th annual edition, and this weekend it returns to Dodger Stadium on November 14th and 15th. The carnival and music festival sold out before the lineup was even unveiled. The carnival and music festival sold out before fans knew who was playing, and the lineup, once revealed, put Don Toliver , Future , Steve Lacy , Turnstile , and Tyler himself at the top. But the sharpest curation happens lower on the bill, where he hands stages to artists the rest of the industry is still catching up to. 
 This year’s crop is a mix of returning faces and first-timers. Rio Amor is a Flog Gnaw veteran, having opened AG Club ’s set in 2023 and the festival in 2024. Last year, Lil Yachty introduced the 20-year-old DJ as the newest member of his Concrete Boys collective. This weekend she plays Flog Gnaw with them for the first time, and she’s promising her opening DJ set “is going to go down in herstory .” For others, the slot is the realization of a childhood dream. London’s Natanya , whose ATTITUDE ERA! mixtape dropped on September 10th, and whose “HUSH” has already been sampled by SZA , calls the lineup slot “a homecoming” after dreaming of the crowd as a kid.  
 Tampa native Gabriel Jacoby bridges soul, blues, and hip-hop, and he’ll make his Flog Gnaw debut almost exactly a year after releasing his first EP, gutta child . He’s bringing unreleased songs to the stage and says he wants to be “an artist people can trust.” North Carolina’s Nomi will also play with a live band for the first time on Sunday, touring songs from her debut EP, this wolf may cry . She hopes festivalgoers watch her and think, “I can do it too.” 
 For a couple of this year’s acts, the weekend closes out a big run. 54 Ultra , the project of New Jersey native Johnny Rodriguez, weaves synthy indie rock and soul with a Latin throughline. He has spent the last year selling out shows around the world after releasing his debut EP, First Works , and sees Flog Gnaw as “a perfect cap” to his first full year of touring. He’ll release a new song the night before and debut it raw with a live band. LA native Quadeca , the mind behind Scrapyard and Vanisher, Horizon Scraper , is treating his set as a “culmination performance of everything leading up to it,” with something weirder promised after. 
 Ahead of the festival, Hypebeast caught up with six emerging artists about what Flog Gnaw means to them, the songs they’re debuting live, and the impressions they hope to leave on the crowd. Below, Rio Amor, Natanya, Gabriel Jacoby, Nomi, 54 Ultra, and Quadeca talk through their festival jitters and make the case for catching your new favorite artist this weekend, before everybody else does. 
 Photo: @caalvinoo 
 Rio Amor 
 Rio Amor has been part of Camp Flog Gnaw’s story longer than most of this year’s lineup. The LA-based DJ opened for Bay Area rap collective AG Club in 2023, then opened the main stage with her own set in 2024. The following year, Lil Yachty introduced the 20-year-old as the newest member of his Concrete Boys crew, a group she first met at the festival. Now their resident DJ, she’ll play Flog Gnaw alongside them for the first time, which she calls “a dream come true” after years of watching them as a fan. 
 On the side, Rio is building her next chapter. She’s producing and writing a project of her own while playing solo shows across the US, which she describes as a “brain dump.” Before Lil Yachty and the Concrete Boys take over, she’s locked in on her opening set, which she vows will go down in “herstory.” Her goal for Flog Gnaw is simple: send the crowd home feeling like they had a blast. 
 HYPEBEAST: How does it feel to return to Camp Flog Gnaw, this time with the Concrete Boys? 
 Rio Amor: It’s so cool because I met all of the Concrete Boys at the festival, and I feel like Flog Gnaw is such a magical place. I was such a big fan of them, and I was like, “I can only imagine what it’d be like if I could get on this stage with them one day.” I just admired their performances so much. To me, this is a dream come true to perform at my favorite festival with my brothers. 
 Where are you in your career right now, and what does this opportunity represent for you?  
 I’m in a very pivotal stage in my career. I haven’t said this out loud to anybody other than my team, but I’ve been working on my own music recently. I’m not singing or rapping, but I’ve been producing and writing since I was a kid, and I’m finally getting to put it into a project of my own, which is very exciting, and I’m learning so much.  
 Alongside that, I’m doing these solo shows, where I just get to brain dump, which is great for my mental health because I just throw all my shit on the stage and roll with it. It’s really fun. I’m so lucky because I get to do that hand in hand with performing with Boat and the boys.  
 When I was younger, I didn’t think that there was any job for me because I didn’t know math or science, but now that I’ve found my thing, it just feels so good, and it means the world to me that I get to do the best thing every day.  
 Three things on your rider 
 A crudité board and coconut water. I can’t really eat before shows, so that’s the only thing that I can stomach. I get really stressed out, and I can take down a crudité board. I always get chips and guac because I feel like people like to eat that. I’m kind of a people pleaser, so when I’m writing my rider, I’m like, “What would everybody else want besides me?” 
 I heard a story of somebody getting an 11×9 picture of Jessica Alba framed on their desk that they need all the time. I was like, “Damn, I should start doing annoying shit like that.” 
 Photo: @caalvinoo 
 Three things you’re packing for the festival? 
 A jacket because it gets cold at night. I always bring hand sanitizer. We’re shaking a lot of hands, and we’re sweating. I don’t play about my hand sanitizer. I bring my friends. That’s like the biggest essential for me. It’s in LA, I live in LA, so it’s my one opportunity to really bring everyone I possibly can and cause issues when I’m sending in my list.  
 Are you doing anything special for this crowd, like new Concrete songs, your own music, special guests, different set lists? 
 I’m really stoked for it because I’ve had a lot of creative input on it. Camo, one of my best friends, is dropping some music really soon, so he has some bangers that he’ll play. The other boys are also on their game, so I know we’re gonna play some unreleased stuff. Karrah just came back to the group, so that’s an exciting piece. 
 I told my team that my 10-minute DJ set before is going to go down in “herstory.” Nobody’s 10-minute DJ set is going to be as good as this one. I am really locked in on it, and maybe some special guests, who knows? 
 What do you want someone seeing you for the first time to walk away feeling? 
 Like they had a blast. I really just love when I see kids being like, “Damn, that shit was fun.” Our sets are super energy-driven, and when I see that rubbed off on them, it’s the best feeling in the world. That’s why I do it. 
 Photo: Tally Francis 
 Natanya 
 Natanya , the 24-year-old singer-songwriter and producer from North London, fuses R&B, alt-pop, neo-soul, jazz, and Caribbean influences into what she calls an “unboxable sound.” She’s been building toward Flog Gnaw for years, from her 2023 EP, Sorrow Sunrise , to Feline’s Return in June 2025. Her latest mixtape, ATTITUDE ERA! , dropped on September 10th, and SZA has already sampled its single “HUSH.” 
 She calls the booking “a homecoming,” the fulfillment of a dream she’s had since she was a kid, and she hopes the crowd leaves trusting that she’ll go far. Her rider is simple: tea, honey, and the strawberries she’s obsessed with. She’s also packing a “gargantuan” makeup bag and an iPad loaded with ROBLOX. She’s keeping her set under wraps so she doesn’t ruin the fun, but she wants every fan to walk away as excited as she is for what comes next. 
 How did you find out you were on the lineup? Did Tyler reach out directly? 
 Natanya: I got a string of lovely WhatsApp messages from my agents all hyping me up! 
 Where are you in your career right now, and what does this opportunity represent for you? 
 I’ve uncovered so much, but still have so far to go. This feels like a homecoming. I’ve dreamed of being in the audience since I was a kid. No idea how I even made it to the stage. I can’t wait to see everyone’s faces in LA! 
 Three things on your rider? 
 I’m such a little prefect. I have my tea and honey sorted, but I love some strawberries. I’m OBSESSED. 
 Three things you’re packing for the festival? 
 My gargantuan makeup bag, my iPad (ROBLOX downloaded, of course), and my iPhone 5C.  
 Are you doing anything special for this crowd, like new songs, guests, or a different setlist? 
 I can’t tell you that or else I’d ruin the fun! 
 What do you want someone seeing you for the first time to walk away feeling? 
 To trust that I’m gonna go far. These moments are so defining for artists like me. I want people to feel excited for the rest of the journey!  
 Photo: Brendon Burton 
 Quadeca 
 Quadeca , born Benjamin Lasky in Los Angeles in 2000, went from internet rap fame to becoming one of the most acclaimed genre-benders of his generation. His self-produced 2024 mixtape, Scrapyard , which compiled his three Scrapyard EPs, drew wide acclaim. He followed it in 2025 with Vanisher, Horizon Scraper , an album featuring Danny Brown , Olēka, and Maruja. Quadeca says he’s at a crossroads, so he’s treating Camp Flog Gnaw as “a culmination performance of everything leading up to it,” and he’s promising something weird afterward. 
 His rider has become a cult favorite among his crew. It includes tea tree toothpicks, which he bulk orders and gets everyone around him hooked on, plus honey Just Ice Tea and, ideally, water. He’s coy about his set and only answered “yes” when I asked about new songs or guests. What he wants is for the crowd to leave in awe of the “boundlessness of music.” 
 How did you find out you were on the lineup? Did Tyler reach out directly? 
 Quadeca: My booking agent was like, “Hey, good news. Do you want to do it? I was like, “Yeah, of course.” 
 Where are you in your career right now? What do you think this opportunity represents for you?  
 I feel like I’m at a crossroads, so I’m viewing Camp Flog Gnaw as a culmination performance of everything leading up to it. Then after the festival, I’m really gonna do some weird shit. 
 Photo: Brendon Burton 
 Three things on your rider. 
 Tea tree toothpicks, I’m addicted to those. I get everybody else hooked on them. Everybody who ever tries one gets addicted, so you have to be careful.  
 Just Ice Tea, honey variant. Shit’s fire. Water. Sometimes there’s no water though, and I’m like, “Damn, do you want me to sing or not?” I don’t get it. 
 When they have the toothpicks, that’s the best venue ever. I bulk order them, like if there’s an apocalypse, at least I have my toothpicks. That’ll keep me grounded.  
 Three things you’re packing for the festival.  
 A gun, a bomb, and music equipment.  
 Are you doing anything special for this set? New songs, guests, different set lists?  
 Yes. 
 What do you want someone seeing you for the first time to walk away feeling? 
 I want them to feel excited and inspired by the boundlessness of music. My set goes to a lot of places, but it still feels like a cohesive vision. The artists there, or people who just enjoy art — I hope that they connect to the music. 
 Photo: Akbar Khan 
 Nomi 
 Nomi , a North Carolina-raised singer-songwriter and DJ, first surfaced last year with 09.30 , a collection of singles built on warm guitar chords and soft, layered vocals. Her debut EP, this wolf may cry , dropped just a few weeks ago, and she calls her Flog Gnaw booking “a miracle.” She writes on instinct and works out the meaning later, and she says she feels like she’s only just stepping onto the stage. 
 She’s already proven herself “to the person that it matters to the most,” and now she wants everyone else to see that she deserves the spot. For the festival, she’s packing “a fire outfit” and throat spray, and her rider calls for fruit, tea, and maybe a bottle of tequila. She’ll perform with a live band for the first time and wants the crowd to watch her and think, “I can do it too.” 
 How did you find out you were on the lineup, and did Tyler reach out directly? 
 Nomi: I was in a meeting with my team, and something annoying had just happened that day, and I was really frustrated. As soon as I surrendered, my manager Figs was like, “Yo, you’re not gonna believe this.” It was 15 seconds later that I see the Flog Gnaw offer, and we just screamed. I couldn’t believe it, it was honestly a miracle. 
 Where are you in your career right now, and what does this opportunity represent for you? 
 I feel like I’m just stepping on stage, and I feel like I have a lot of eyes on me, and I’m just ready to show myself. I’ve already proven myself to the person that it matters to the most, which is me. I really just want to show people that I want to be here, and that I deserve to be there.  
 Three things on your rider? 
 I’ll always have fruit and tea for sure. I may or may not just be like, “Yo, just throw in a little bottle of tequila.”  
 Three things you’re packing for the festival? 
 Throat spray, a fire outfit, and my in-ears. 
 Are you doing anything special for this crowd?   
 Definitely. I’m gonna perform my songs with a live band for the first time.  
 What do you want someone seeing you for the first time to walk away feeling? 
 I want them to see themselves in me and think “I can do it too,” or “that’s really cool that somebody can be brave like that.”  
 Photo: Kyle Keli'ikoa 
 54 Ultra 
 54 Ultra is the solo project of New Jersey native Johnny Rodriguez, a producer and singer-songwriter who blends garage pop and soul with indie rock influences and a Latin throughline. Since releasing his debut EP, First Works , in May 2025, he has sold out shows around the world. He calls Camp Flog Gnaw a “sensitive” moment in his career because he’s still introducing himself to so many people, and he sees the festival as “a perfect cap” to his first year of touring. 
 He’s watched Flog Gnaw performances for years, and now he’s ready to be the one inspiring others. For the weekend, he’s packing platform shoes, his guitar, and maybe a nice jacket to eat his pistachios in, since I told him Rio said it gets cold at night. He’s debuting new music, including a song that drops the night before, and describes the set as a “straight live situation.” He wants the audience to leave inspired, as if they’d stumbled onto a nice surprise. 
 How did you find out you were on the lineup, and did Tyler reach out directly? 
 54 Ultra: My team. An offer came in, and I saw the flyer, and that’s where I really confirmed it. It wasn’t Tyler directly, but I don’t blame him. I can’t wait to meet him, hopefully, I can say “hi” or something. 
 Where are you in your career right now, and what does this opportunity represent for you? 
 It’s definitely a sensitive part of my career because I’m still introducing myself to so many people, and having done other festivals this year, Flog Gnaw seems like a perfect cap to the first year of really touring and being on a public scale. I’m excited to do it because I’ve watched those performances before, and I’ve been influenced by Flog Gnaw, so I can’t wait to be that guy for people now.  
 Photo: Max Tardio 
 Three things on your rider? 
 A fruit plate, a protein shake, and pistachios with the shell. 
 Three things you’re packing for the festival? 
 Platform shoes, my guitar, and maybe a nice jacket.  
 Are you doing anything special for this crowd? New songs, guests, different set lists? 
 We’re definitely doing new music. A new song will be released the night before, so that’ll be fun. It’s gonna be very raw because it’s gonna be a live band — a straight live situation. 
 What do you want someone seeing you for the first time to walk away feeling? 
 I want them to feel inspired and happy that they saw me, like a nice surprise. I want them to feel like, “Oh wow, we actually started paying attention for this.” 
 Photo: Josh Flores 
 Gabriel Jacoby 
 Meet this year’s “gutta child” from the “dirty south.” Tampa native Gabriel Jacoby bridges soul, blues, and hip-hop, a sound he’s been building since 2022 with singles like “ the one ,” “ baby ,” “ be careful ,” and “ forever ,” each of which has surpassed a million streams. He followed them last November with his debut EP, gutta child . Tyler didn’t reach out directly about the booking, but Gabriel says the festival founder has messaged him before to compliment his music, which adds Tyler to a list of co-signs that already includes Dominic Fike and Justin Bieber . 
 He calls Flog Gnaw “a big deal” and a chance to put his art in front of people who may never have been exposed to someone like him. His rider includes a bowl of fruit, herbal tea, and sometimes wine, and he’s packing his nebulizer, his digital camera, and “a good attitude.” This weekend, he’s debuting unreleased songs due out in the next few months, and he says the way they’re rehearsing the set is “unlike anything we’ve done before.” He wants Flog Gnaw’s young crowd to feel relieved, like they can breathe, and to see him as an artist they can trust. 
 How did you find out you’re on the lineup? Did Tyler reach out directly? 
 Gabriel Jacoby: Pertaining to Flog Gnaw, he did not, but he has reached out before, just to compliment my music. I found out through my team, just working with my label.  
 Where are you in your career right now, and what does this opportunity represent for you? 
 Definitely a big deal. Definitely something I always looked forward to doing if I ever got the chance, and so now that I have the chance, [I’m] very grateful. I see it as a way to put my art in front of people that may have never been exposed to someone like me. 
 Photo: Courtesy of Gabriel Jacoby 
 Three things on your rider? 
 A bowl of fruit, sometimes wine, and any kind of herbal tea. Gotta soothe the throat for the singing.  
 Three things you’re packing for Flog Gnaw? 
 Definitely my nebulizer, my digital camera, and a good attitude.  
 Are you doing anything special for this crowd? Like new songs, guests, different set lists. 
 I’ll be playing a couple of unreleased things that are gonna be coming out in the next few months. This set will be very fresh, like the way we’re rehearsing is unlike anything we’ve done before. I wanted to bring something brand new.  
 What do you want someone seeing you for the first time to walk away feeling? 
 I want people to feel relieved, like they can breathe. I always like to see myself as an artist people can trust. No matter if you resonate with what I’m saying or not, I can say something that matters. Camp Flog Gnaw has a lot of young people there, so doing and saying the right thing, and uplifting people as much as I can is important. 
 Camp Flog Gnaw Carnival takes place on November 14th and 15th at Dodger Stadium in Los Angeles, California.
